title: Acid-base and ABG
summary: Interpret any blood gas in five steps (pH, primary process, compensation, anion gap with albumin correction, delta ratio), work up high and normal anion gap acidosis, metabolic alkalosis and respiratory disorders, recognise mixed disorders, and know when a venous gas is enough.

topics.title: Five-step blood gas interpretation
topics.summary: 1) Acidaemia or alkalaemia? 2) Primary process (look at PaCO2 and HCO3-). 3) Is compensation appropriate? 4) Anion gap (correct for albumin). 5) If HAGMA, the delta ratio reveals hidden disorders. Then the clinical story.

steps.title: pH
steps.detail: < 7.35 acidaemia, > 7.45 alkalaemia. A normal pH does not exclude a mixed disorder.

steps.title: Primary process
steps.detail: pH low + HCO3- low = metabolic acidosis; pH low + PaCO2 high = respiratory acidosis; pH high + HCO3- high = metabolic alkalosis; pH high + PaCO2 low = respiratory alkalosis.

steps.title: Compensation
steps.detail: Metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3- + 8 (± 2) (Winters). Metabolic alkalosis: PaCO2 rises ~0.7 per 1 mmol/L HCO3- rise. Respiratory: see the compensation table. Outside range = second disorder.

steps.title: Anion gap
steps.detail: AG = Na+ − (Cl- + HCO3-); normal ≈ 8-12 (analyser-dependent). Corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (40 − albumin g/L)/10, i.e. + 2.5 per 10 g/L fall in albumin.

steps.title: Delta ratio
steps.detail: (AG − 12) ÷ (24 − HCO3-). < 0.4 = NAGMA; 0.4-0.8 = mixed HAGMA + NAGMA; 0.8-2 = pure HAGMA; > 2 = HAGMA + metabolic alkalosis (or pre-existing high HCO3-).

steps.title: Oxygenation
steps.detail: A-a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2, where PAO2 = FiO2 × (760 − 47) − PaCO2/0.8. Normal ≈ age/4 + 4 on room air.

tables.title: Expected compensation
rows: PaCO2 rises 0.7 mmHg per 1 mmol/L HCO3- rise
HCO3- rises 1 per 10 mmHg PaCO2 rise
HCO3- rises 3.5-4 per 10 mmHg PaCO2 rise

redFlags.text: Metabolic acidosis with PaCO2 higher than predicted: respiratory failure is imminent (tiring).

pitfalls.text: Forgetting albumin correction: hypoalbuminaemia hides a raised anion gap.
Mixing mmHg and kPa (1 kPa = 7.5 mmHg).

pearls.text: Quick check: in pure metabolic acidosis, PaCO2 (mmHg) ≈ the last two digits of pH (e.g. pH 7.25 → PaCO2 ~25).

nodes.text: Acidaemia: HCO3- low (metabolic) or PaCO2 high (respiratory)?
Alkalaemia: HCO3- high (metabolic) or PaCO2 low (respiratory)?
Normal pH: check PaCO2 and HCO3- for a hidden mixed disorder
Metabolic acidosis: Winters check, anion gap (albumin-corrected), delta ratio
Respiratory disorder: acute vs chronic compensation
Integrate with the clinical story; treat causes

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: The bicarbonate-CO2 buffer system follows Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = 6.1 + log(HCO3- / 0.03 × PaCO2). The Stewart approach (strong ion difference, weak acids, PaCO2) explains chloride and albumin effects and is complementary.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Berend 2014:** physiological (bicarbonate-based) approach with compensation rules, anion gap and delta ratio.
- **Figge 1998:** each 10 g/L fall in albumin lowers the anion gap by ~2.5 mmol/L.
consultantNotes.controversies: - Physiological vs Stewart vs base-excess approaches give similar bedside conclusions when applied correctly.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Hypoalbuminaemia (malnutrition, chronic liver disease, sepsis) is very common in Indian ICUs; always correct the anion gap.

topics.title: High anion gap metabolic acidosis
topics.summary: Lactate, ketones, uraemia and toxins cause most HAGMA. Measure lactate, ketones, creatinine, glucose and serum osmolality; an osmolal gap > 10-20 points to toxic alcohols. Treat the cause; bicarbonate only for selected severe cases.

steps.title: First line
steps.detail: Lactate, blood ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate), glucose, urea/creatinine, CK, paracetamol and salicylate levels, serum osmolality.

steps.title: GOLDMARK
steps.detail: Glycols, Oxoproline (paracetamol), L-lactate, D-lactate, Methanol, Aspirin, Renal failure, Ketoacidosis (diabetic, alcoholic, starvation).

steps.title: Toxic alcohols
steps.detail: Measured − calculated osmolality (2Na + glucose/18 + urea/2.8 in mg/dL units, or 2Na + glucose + urea in mmol/L). Gap > 10-20 with HAGMA: methanol or ethylene glycol until proven otherwise.

steps.title: Cause first
steps.detail: Lactate: perfusion, sepsis, thiamine; DKA: insulin/fluids; uraemia: dialysis; methanol/EG: fomepizole or ethanol + haemodialysis.

steps.title: Selected
steps.detail: pH ≤ 7.20 with moderate-severe AKI (AKIN 2-3): bicarbonate to pH ≥ 7.30 reduced dialysis need and mortality in that subgroup (BICAR-ICU). Not routine for lactic acidosis.

doseCards.dose: 4.2% 125-250 mL over 30 min, repeat to pH ≥ 7.30 (max 1 L/24 h) – BICAR-ICU
doseCards.workedExample: Deficit 70 kg, HCO3- 8 → target 16: 0.5 × 70 × 8 = 280 mmol; give ~140 mmol then re-check

doseCards.dose: 15 mg/kg load, then 10 mg/kg every 12 h

redFlags.text: HAGMA + visual blurring after illicit liquor: methanol (Indian hooch tragedies) → ethanol/fomepizole + urgent dialysis.
HAGMA with normal lactate and ketones in a patient on paracetamol (malnourished, sepsis): 5-oxoproline.

pitfalls.text: Treating lactic acidosis with bicarbonate alone (no outcome benefit; worsens intracellular acidosis).
Euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors (glucose < 250 mg/dL).

pearls.text: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: often normal glucose, mixed alkalosis from vomiting; treat with dextrose, thiamine and fluids, not insulin.

nodes.text: Lactic acidosis: perfusion, sepsis, ischaemia, drugs, thiamine

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Kraut & Madias 2010, 2014:** causes and management of metabolic and lactic acidosis.
- **BICAR-ICU (2018):** bicarbonate in severe metabolic acidaemia: no overall mortality difference, but lower mortality and dialysis in patients with AKIN 2-3.
consultantNotes.controversies: - Bicarbonate in DKA (generally not unless pH < 6.9-7.0).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Methanol mass poisonings from illicit liquor recur in India; ethanol is the practical antidote and early haemodialysis is critical.
- Fomepizole is generally unavailable.

topics.title: Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis
topics.summary: NAGMA comes from bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea, fistula, ureteric diversion), renal tubular acidosis, or chloride loading (large volumes of 0.9% saline). The urine anion gap separates GI from renal causes.

steps.title: Obvious cause?
steps.detail: Diarrhoea, pancreatic/biliary fistula, ileal conduit, large saline infusions, acetazolamide, recovery phase of DKA.

steps.title: Urine anion gap
steps.detail: UAG = urine Na+ + K+ − Cl-. Negative (−20 to −50) = appropriate NH4+ excretion (GI loss). Positive = impaired renal acid excretion (distal RTA, CKD).

steps.title: RTA
steps.detail: Type 1 (distal): urine pH > 5.5, hypokalaemia, stones. Type 2 (proximal): bicarbonaturia, Fanconi. Type 4: hyperkalaemia (hypoaldosteronism, diabetes, drugs).

steps.title: Cause + bicarbonate
steps.detail: Replace losses with balanced solutions; oral or IV bicarbonate for ongoing losses or RTA; correct K+ before bicarbonate in hypokalaemia.

redFlags.text: Severe hypokalaemia with NAGMA (distal RTA, diarrhoea): correct K+ before alkali to avoid worsening hypokalaemia.

pitfalls.text: Repeated 0.9% saline boluses causing hyperchloraemic acidosis that is then misread as ongoing shock.

pearls.text: Ringer's lactate or Plasma-Lyte limit hyperchloraemia during resuscitation.

nodes.text: Metabolic acidosis with normal corrected AG
Treat cause; balanced fluids; bicarbonate if severe
Low/normal K+: distal or proximal RTA; nephrology

consultantNotes.evidence: - **Kraut & Madias 2010:** urine anion gap and RTA classification.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Acute diarrhoeal disease (including cholera) is a common cause of severe NAGMA with hypokalaemia in Indian ICUs, especially in monsoon months.

quiz.explanation: Chloride load lowers the strong ion difference.

topics.title: Metabolic alkalosis
topics.summary: Usually from vomiting/NG losses, diuretics or post-hypercapnia. Urine chloride separates chloride-responsive (< 20 mmol/L) from chloride-resistant causes. Treat with chloride, potassium and volume; acetazolamide if overloaded.

steps.title: Common ICU causes
steps.detail: NG drainage, vomiting, loop/thiazide diuretics, post-hypercapnic (after ventilating chronic CO2 retainers), citrate (massive transfusion, CRRT), hypokalaemia, steroids/mineralocorticoid excess.

steps.title: Urine chloride
steps.detail: < 20 mmol/L = chloride-responsive (vomiting, past diuretics). > 40 mmol/L = current diuretics, mineralocorticoid excess, severe hypokalaemia, Bartter/Gitelman.

steps.title: Chloride-responsive
steps.detail: 0.9% saline if volume-depleted, KCl to K+ ≥ 4; PPI for ongoing NG loss.

steps.title: Overloaded
steps.detail: Acetazolamide 250-500 mg IV once or twice daily (watch K+); reduce loop diuretic; KCl.

steps.title: pH > 7.55-7.6
steps.detail: Consider dilute HCl (central line) or dialysis with low-bicarbonate bath (rare).

redFlags.text: pH > 7.55 with hypokalaemia: arrhythmia risk; hypoventilation may impede weaning.

pitfalls.text: Normalising PaCO2 quickly in a chronic CO2 retainer (post-hypercapnic alkalosis).

pearls.text: 'It is chloride depletion alkalosis, not contraction alkalosis' (Luke & Galla).

consultantNotes.evidence: - **Luke & Galla 2012:** chloride depletion maintains alkalosis; chloride repletion corrects it.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with high urine chloride and normal BP in young adults: consider Gitelman syndrome or surreptitious diuretic use.

topics.title: Respiratory acidosis and alkalosis
topics.summary: Respiratory acidosis means alveolar hypoventilation: think drive (drugs, brain), pump (neuromuscular, chest wall, fatigue) or lungs (COPD, asthma). Respiratory alkalosis is hyperventilation from hypoxaemia, sepsis, pain, PE, liver failure, salicylates or pregnancy.

steps.title: Acute or chronic?
steps.detail: Use the compensation rules: acute HCO3- +1 per 10 mmHg, chronic +3.5-4 per 10.

steps.title: Find the cause
steps.detail: Sedatives/opioids (naloxone), neuromuscular weakness (GBS, MG, snake envenomation, organophosphates), obesity hypoventilation, COPD/asthma, ventilator settings.

steps.title: Treat
steps.detail: Reverse drugs, NIV for COPD/obesity, intubate for coma or exhaustion; in ventilated patients increase minute ventilation (except permissive hypercapnia strategies).

steps.title: Find the cause
steps.detail: Hypoxaemia, sepsis (early), PE, pain/anxiety, CNS lesions, liver failure, salicylate toxicity (mixed with HAGMA), pregnancy, over-ventilation on the ventilator.

steps.title: Treat the cause
steps.detail: Do not rebreathe into a bag; hypoxaemia must be excluded first.

redFlags.text: Rising PaCO2 in neuromuscular weakness: late sign; check vital capacity (< 15-20 mL/kg → intubate).
Respiratory alkalosis + HAGMA in an adult: salicylate poisoning.

pitfalls.text: Assuming hyperventilation is anxiety without excluding PE, sepsis, DKA or hypoxaemia.

pearls.text: Normal PaCO2 in acute severe asthma is a danger sign (fatigue).

nodes.text: Vital capacity and NIF; early intubation if failing
Lung/airway disease: bronchodilators, NIV, ventilator strategy

consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Neurotoxic snakebite (krait, cobra) and organophosphate poisoning are major causes of acute respiratory acidosis in rural India (modules 28-29).

topics.title: Mixed disorders and when a VBG is enough
topics.summary: Suspect a mixed disorder when compensation is outside the expected range, the delta ratio is abnormal, or the pH is normal with abnormal PaCO2 and HCO3-. A venous gas is adequate for pH, HCO3-, lactate and electrolytes, but not for PaO2 or (often) PaCO2.

steps.title: Mixed clues
steps.detail: Normal pH with abnormal values; compensation off by > 2-3 mmHg; delta ratio < 0.8 or > 2.

steps.title: Common combos
steps.detail: Sepsis with vomiting (HAGMA + metabolic alkalosis); DKA + diarrhoea (HAGMA + NAGMA); COPD + diuretics (respiratory acidosis + metabolic alkalosis); salicylate (respiratory alkalosis + HAGMA); cardiac arrest (respiratory + metabolic acidosis).

steps.title: Agreement
steps.detail: Venous pH ≈ arterial − 0.03; HCO3- ≈ arterial + 1; venous PCO2 ~4-6 mmHg higher but wide limits; venous PO2 is not useful. Normal venous PCO2 (< 45) reliably excludes arterial hypercapnia.

steps.title: When
steps.detail: Need PaO2 (oxygenation targets, P/F), shock with poor perfusion (VBG diverges), suspected hypercapnia needing precise values, and ventilator adjustments.

redFlags.text: Normal pH with very high PaCO2 and high HCO3- in an acutely ill patient can mask a new acute process.

pitfalls.text: Using venous PO2 to judge oxygenation.

pearls.text: A VBG plus pulse oximetry answers most questions in a stable patient and spares an arterial puncture.

nodes.text: Need precise oxygenation (P/F, PaO2 targets) or in shock?
Confirm hypercapnia with ABG if decisions depend on it

consultantNotes.evidence: - **Kelly 2010:** venous pH and bicarbonate agree closely with arterial values; PCO2 agreement is too wide for substitution but normal venous PCO2 screens out hypercapnia.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Arterial gas syringes and analyser cartridges are costly; VBG strategies reduce cost and patient discomfort.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.indications: Severe metabolic acidaemia (pH ≤ 7.20) with moderate-severe AKI (BICAR-ICU); hyperkalaemia with acidosis; sodium-channel blocker toxicity; NAGMA with ongoing bicarbonate loss; urinary alkalinisation (salicylate, rhabdomyolysis).
drugs.adultDose: Bolus 50-100 mmol IV, or infusion titrated to pH > 7.30 (BICAR-ICU: 4.2% 125-250 mL over 30 min, max 1 L/24 h). Bicarbonate deficit (mmol) ≈ 0.5 × weight (kg) × (target − measured HCO3-); give half over hours and re-check.
drugs.preparationIndia: 7.5% (0.9 mmol/mL) and 8.4% (1 mmol/mL) 10 mL and 25 mL ampoules; isotonic 1.4% can be made as 150 mL of 8.4% in 850 mL D5W/water (≈ 150 mmol/L).
drugs.cautions: Hypernatraemia, volume overload, hypokalaemia, ionised hypocalcaemia, raised CO2 (needs ventilation to clear), tissue necrosis on extravasation.

drugs.name: Thiamine
drugs.indications: Suspected thiamine deficiency (alcohol use, malnutrition, unexplained lactic acidosis, Wernicke's).
drugs.adultDose: 200-500 mg IV three times daily for 3-5 days in suspected Wernicke's; 100-200 mg IV daily for prophylaxis.
drugs.preparationIndia: 100 mg/mL ampoules (often 1 mL or 10 mL vials).
drugs.cautions: Rare anaphylaxis; give before glucose in at-risk patients.

drugs.name: Fomepizole / ethanol
drugs.adultDose: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV load, then 10 mg/kg every 12 h (increase during dialysis). If unavailable: oral or IV ethanol to blood level 100-150 mg/dL (loading ~0.8 g/kg).
drugs.preparationIndia: Fomepizole is rarely available in India; ethanol (oral 40% spirits via NG tube or IV 10% in D5) is used.
drugs.cautions: Ethanol: hypoglycaemia, sedation; needs frequent levels. Haemodialysis is definitive for severe poisoning.
drugs.verify: Ethanol dosing in India is protocol-dependent; see module 27.

verify.reason: Normal anion gap depends on the analyser (with or without K+; modern ion-selective analysers often 4-12 mmol/L). Use local ranges.
